title: [Editorial] Coasting on artificial intelligence safety
desc: Colluding on unsanctioned message boards and infiltrating a technology platform. Hacking the statistics portal of a health care scheme. Accessing and modifying personal data and business invoices. These are just a few examples from the past year of publicly reported systems breaches by artificial intelligence (AI) agents. Such reports have heightened some people's concerns that AI poses an existential threat, with others dismissing such concerns as marketing hype. What is not debatable is that AI agents are rapidly evolving, potentially beyond human containment.

title: Challenges for human oversight in detecting system malfunctions in AI-assisted medical diagnostics
desc: Increasingly, physicians must oversee AI systems to detect system malfunctions. We studied 48 physicians in a randomized controlled study using an increasingly malfunctioning AI for cardiac auscultation. Diagnostic performance declined alongside AI reliability, even when physicians were cognitively forced to make an initial classification, and when human performance exceeded AI reliability. Physicians’ confidence declined faster than their trust in AI. Results call for specification of oversight goals and processes ensuring patient safety.

title: Artificial intelligence-driven precision management of Helicobacter pylori: an integrated framework from endoscopy and multi-omics to vaccine design and digital care.
source: PubMed · Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
desc: [Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology] Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection, affecting half of the world's population, is the principal cause of peptic ulcer disease and gastric cancer, yet its clinical management is increasingly undermined by the rapidly escalating global burden of antibiotic resistance, the suboptimal accuracy of conventional diagnostic methods, and the declining efficacy of empirical therapeutic regimens. Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping this landscape, but existing research remains fragmented across single modalities. We propose a conceptual five-module framework that integrates AI approaches across the H. pylori care continuum: (1) global disease burden and the evolutionary dynamics of H. pylori drug resistance; (2) the application of multimodal AI, from convolutional neural networks to vision-language foundation models, for endoscopic early screening, pathological identification, and functional assessment; (3) the harnessing of machine learning (ML) on genomic and electronic health record data to decipher resistance mechanisms and generate personalized eradication regimens; (4) AI-driven vaccine target discovery and generative design, spanning reverse vaccinology to de novo immunogen creation; and (5) a digital closed-loop patient management platform that leverages new media and reinforcement learning to enhance adherence and eradication rates. We further delineate the core challenges of data bias, cross-scenario generalization, and the critical absence of prospective randomized evidence, and propose a future direction anchored in multimodal foundation models, federated learning, and continuous AI quality improvement. Rather than an established clinical pathway, this framework is proposed as a conceptual blueprint that, once prospectively validated, could upgrade AI-enabled H. pylori care from isolated image recognition toward an end-to-end "perception-reasoning-intervention" system, offering a blueprint for precision prevention and control.

title: Pathological Micro-Niches and Multimodal Imaging Macro-Niches for Predicting Clinically Significant Prostate Cancer and Metastasis: A Multicenter Study
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Guangxi Medical University; conditions: Prostate Cancer, Prostatic Neoplasms; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 2000; status: ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING] This is an investigator-initiated, multicenter, observational ambispective cohort study, predominantly retrospective, with an optional prospective non-interventional silent validation. The study tests a cross-scale hypothesis that the pathological micro-niche of the primary prostate tumor (tumor epithelium, invasive front, immune-rich or immune-poor regions, ECM/collagen remodeling, neurovascular neighborhoods, and peritumoral field effect) is associated at the patient level with the imaging macro-niche captured by multiparametric MRI (diffusion, perfusion, heterogeneity, local invasion) and PSMA PET/CT (receptor expression, whole-body lesion distribution, tumor burden). A pathology teacher model provides patient- or lesion-set-level niche representations only during model development; at deployment and validation, only MRI, PSMA PET/CT, and clinical information available before the prediction time point are used, with no voxel-level pathology-to-imaging registration. Under one master protocol with three pre-specified substudies, the system predicts: (A) patient- and lesion-level clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa, ISUP Grade Group 2 or higher) from pre-biopsy MRI; (B) pathological pelvic lymph node metastasis (pN1) after radical prostatectomy with pelvic lymph node dissection, primarily from MRI; and (C) concurrent distant metastasis (M1) and subsequent distant metastasis in baseline M0 patients, primarily from PSMA PET/CT. Models are evaluated for discrimination, calibration, clinical net benefit, uncertainty, abstention, and stability across centers, scanners, tracers, and disease spectra, using locked multicenter external validation and prospective silent validation. Model outputs are never shown to clinicians or patients and do not alter care.

title: Evaluating Pretrained Language Semantics for Structured EHR Prediction Tasks
desc: Structured Electronic Health Records (EHR) models typically treat each clinical concept as a dataset-specific token, discarding the natural-language semantics associated with the event. As a result, relationships between concepts must largely be learned from EHR co-occurrence, without directly exploiting any prior semantic knowledge. We investigate how pretrained causal language models can be adapted for longitudinal EHR prediction by developing tEHR. Here, we represent events with their natural language description and use this text stream to apply EHR-adaptive continued pretraining, followed by task-specific discriminative fine-tuning using LoRA, utilising the LLM as a longitudinal patient-encoder. We evaluate this approach across four prediction tasks on the MIMIC-IV dataset and pancreatic cancer prediction on the CPRD dataset at 1 to 12 month horizons, with tEHR using the Mistral-7B-v0.3 backbone achieving the strongest overall performance. Ablations show that performance declines when clinical descriptions are removed or misaligned, when numerical values are omitted, and when either stage of adaptation is removed, while explicit elapsed-time descriptions provide little additional benefit. Analysis of the learned patient representations further reveals clinically coherent structure associated with distinct patterns of disease risk and clinical history.

title: Do Rule-Derived Labels Improve Prediction When Reported Labels Are Limited? A Two-Site Machine Learning Study
desc: **Background.** Rule derived (weak) labels can enlarge a training set when reported labels are scarce. Their value depends on label quality, on how the extra records shift the training distribution, and on whether the comparison accounts for reported labels set aside for tuning or calibration. **Methods.** We ran an exploratory label-budget experiment on *Escherichia coli* urine cultures from two de-identified electronic health record datasets: Stanford ARMD and UT Southwestern ARMD-UTSW. The task was to predict reported non-susceptibility to cefepime, cefoxitin and ceftazidime (Stanford) and to cefepime and ceftazidime (UT Southwestern). Reported-label budgets of 10%, 25%, 50% and 100% of development patients were drawn over five patient-disjoint outer splits. Logistic regression and histogram gradient boosting were trained with reported labels only, or with added rule-derived labels using equal weights, a tuning-selected weight, class-proportion adjustment or prior-probability correction. These were compared with an all-budget reported-only baseline that used every budgeted reported label for training. Stanford used the inferred labels released with the dataset and a feature set including resistance history. UT Southwestern used researcher-derived labels from Stanford rule text, which were not validated for that site, and an age-only primary model. Brier-score differences were assessed with paired patient-cluster bootstrap intervals. **Results.** All rule-derived labels were susceptible. Equal-weight augmentation lowered mean predicted risk well below observed prevalence (for example, Stanford cefepime at the 10% budget: 0.35% versus 4.85%) and had a higher Brier score than the all-budget baseline in every drug, model and budget summary. The tuning-selected weight did not consistently improve on the all-budget baseline. Its median Brier difference was positive in 38 of 40 drug, model and budget summaries. Its paired intervals lay above zero in 100 of 296 Stanford analyses and 31 of 198 UT Southwestern analyses, and below zero in 3 and 5. The tuning set often selected a weight of zero (146 of 296 and 153 of 198 analyses). At UT Southwestern, the age-only models showed little discrimination (median AUROC 0.49 to 0.54), so those comparisons mainly reflect calibration. **Conclusions.** Under these designs, rule-derived labels did not consistently improve probability prediction over a reported-only model that used the whole reported-label budget for training.

title: Bloom unifies brain cell representations across modalities and contexts
desc: Multimodal genomic datasets now profile mammalian brain cells across anatomical regions, developmental stages, disease states, and species. Learning shared representations that capture cellular diversity across these heterogeneous observations remains a central challenge. Here, we introduce Bloom, a transformer-based model that represents cells using gene expression, chromatin accessibility, or both. Bloom is trained on 300,000 adult mouse brain cells with paired measurements, randomly sampled with broad-subclass balancing--approximately 100-fold fewer cells than used by comparable pre-trained models. By combining genomic sequence embeddings with randomly sampled multimodal cell views, Bloom outperforms unimodal cell models in resolving brain-wide cell types and in annotation, regression, and label-transfer tasks. Its attention patterns reveal cell-type-dependent associations among genomic loci, including pairs separated by millions of base pairs. These results establish Bloom as a data-efficient framework for integrating multimodal brain cell measurements and generating hypotheses about cell-type-specific genomic relationships.

[Comment] Mortality prediction using cardiac magnetic resonance: artificial intelligence versus clinicians–Quo vadis?
desc: With a rise in the incidence of cardiovascular disease in ageing populations worldwide, physicians will face a substantial increase in demand for feasible and accurate diagnostics. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) is a highly accurate, non-ionising imaging technique for quantitative assessment of cardiac function and geometry and for detection of cardiovascular diseases. However, CMR lacks the high throughput, low cost, and portability of echocardiography. Another widespread clinical obstacle to CMR is the shortage of qualified and trained operators.
